title: What theory holds the QALY up?

parts.title: The gamble as a ruler
parts.brief: Why the standard gamble's indifference probability is a utility: von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility is the calibration.
parts.figure: A standard-gamble decision tree. A decision node (square) with two branches. Branch 'Certain': a terminal 'State q' (the treated chronic state for life). Branch 'Gamble': a chance node (circle) splitting into 'Full health' (probability p, payoff 1) and 'Death' (probability 1 − p, payoff 0). Beats in order: the decision node and the two branch names appear; the certain branch; the gamble with its two outcomes and their utilities 1 and 0; p is set to 0.7 and written on the branch; the gamble's expected value p × 1 + (1 − p) × 0 = p is folded back to the chance node as 0.7; the certain branch gets q = 0.7 and the two are highlighted as equal. Scratch card: EU = p·1 + (1−p)·0 = p — temporary, gone after line 10. Explore: drag p on the gamble branch and watch the chance node's expected value follow it one for one.
script: What theory lets us read a QALY weight as a person's utility — what is holding that number up?
The easy answer: a weight is just a score for how good a state feels.
Expected utility theory makes a much stronger claim, and the standard gamble shows it.
One branch is certain: live out your life in the treated state.
The other is a gamble: full health with probability p, immediate death otherwise.
We raise p until the person cannot choose between them — say, at p = 0.7.
Why should that indifference point be the weight?
Von Neumann and Morgenstern showed that if choices obey a few axioms, a gamble is worth the probability-weighted average of its outcomes' utilities.
Full health is fixed at 1 and death at 0, so the gamble is worth p times 1 plus one minus p times 0 — exactly p.
Indifference means the certain state is worth the same: q = 0.7.
Pause and drag p: the gamble's value follows it one for one.
The catch is that many people overweight a sure thing, and then p is no longer their utility.
So the weight is a utility exactly as far as the person chooses by expected utility.

parts.title: Adding up rectangles
parts.brief: Pliskin, Shepard and Weinstein (1980): mutual utility independence and constant proportional trade-off make quality a fixed multiplier on years.
parts.figure: A quality-over-time plot drawn as straight segments: quality q (0 to 1) on the y-axis, years t (0 to 10) on the x-axis. Path 'Treated': q = 0.7 for 5 years, its area shaded and labelled '3.5 QALYs'. Path 'Full health': q = 1 for 3.5 years, same area, labelled '3.5'. Then the Treated path is extended to 10 years (the 5-year version left as a faded ghost), its area 7, and the Full health path extended to 7 years. The give-up share '30%' is written as a readout at both durations. Scratch card: 1.5 of 5 = 30%; 3 of 10 = 30% — temporary, gone after line 10.
script: Now that one weight is a utility, can we simply multiply it by years and add?
Pliskin, Shepard and Weinstein asked exactly that in 1980, and answered with conditions on preferences.
Take the treated patient: five years at q = 0.7 — an area of 3.5 QALYs.
The QALY model says this is as good as 3.5 years in full health: equal areas, equal value.
First condition, mutual utility independence: how you rank lengths of life does not depend on the health state, and how you rank states does not depend on the length.
Second, constant proportional trade-off: suppose the patient would give up 1.5 of the 5 years — 30 per cent — to be in full health.
Now make it ten years at 0.7. How many would they give up?
Constant proportional trade-off says 30 per cent again: three years, leaving seven in full health.
The share traded is fixed whatever the duration — that is what makes q a constant multiplier.
For some states people will bear a few years but not many, and then the share is not constant.
Together these two give utility as a quality weight times some function of years; a third condition makes that function the years themselves.
So adding up rectangles is not arithmetic: it is an assumption about how people trade time for quality.

parts.title: Risk neutral about years
parts.brief: The third condition, risk neutrality over life years — and Bleichrodt, Wakker and Johannesson (1997), who showed it suffices on its own for chronic states.
parts.figure: A decision tree for a gamble on length of life, all in the treated state q = 0.7. Decision node with two branches. 'Sure': terminal '5 years', value 3.5 QALYs. 'Coin flip': a chance node splitting into '10 years' (probability 0.5, value 7 QALYs) and 'Death' (probability 0.5, value 0). Beats in order: the sure branch and its 3.5; the coin flip and its outcomes; the chance node's fold-back 0.5 × 7 + 0.5 × 0 = 3.5 written at the node; both branches highlighted as equal (the QALY model is indifferent); then the sure branch highlighted alone as what most people prefer. Readout: 'BWJ 1997: risk neutrality ⇒ QALY' — temporary, appears at line 9, gone after line 11. Explore: drag the coin flip's probability of 10 years and watch its value move while the sure branch stays at 3.5; they meet only at one half.
script: The third condition is the strongest: risk neutrality over life years.
Here is the test, all in the treated state, q = 0.7: five years for sure.
Or a coin flip: ten years with probability one half, immediate death otherwise.
The QALY model scores the sure branch at 3.5 QALYs.
And the flip? Half of 7 plus half of 0 is 3.5 — exactly the same.
So the QALY model says you should not care which you get. Would you really flip that coin?
Most people would not: studies usually find people risk averse about the length of their life.
For them a QALY is not their utility — it rates the gamble as highly as the sure five years they prefer.
Bleichrodt, Wakker and Johannesson showed in 1997 how much hangs on this one condition.
For chronic states, risk neutrality over life years — plus the zero condition, that zero years are worth the same in every health state — is enough on its own; the other conditions follow.
Pause and drag the flip's probability: its value moves, the sure branch stays at 3.5, and they meet only at one half.
So the QALY as a utility stands or falls with one testable attitude to risk — and few people quite hold it.

parts.title: Welfare or health?
parts.brief: Welfarism versus extra-welfarism (Culyer): whether the QALY must be a utility at all — the synthesis of the lecture.
parts.figure: A two-column comparison table built row by row, columns 'Welfarism' and 'Extra-welfarism'. Rows, one per beat: 'Counts' — 'Own utility' | 'Health'; 'Measure' — 'WTP' | 'QALY'; 'Method' — 'CBA' | 'CEA'; 'Needs' — 'EU conditions' | 'Agreed measure'. The Welfarism column fills first, then Extra-welfarism. Then the 'Needs' row is highlighted as the difference that matters. Scratch card: the running example, ΔQ = 1.5, ΔC = 30,000, ICER = 20,000 vs λ — temporary, appears at line 9, gone after line 10. At the end both column headers are highlighted together as the two foundations.
script: Now that the utility foundation looks thin, ask what the QALY is for.
Two answers split health economics. The first, welfarism: what counts is each person's own utility, as they judge it.
Its natural tool is cost–benefit analysis, with benefits valued by willingness to pay.
For a welfarist, the conditions of this lecture are essential: a QALY that is not a utility does not measure welfare.
The second answer is extra-welfarism, a term associated with Anthony Culyer, drawing on Amartya Sen.
Here health itself is the social goal a decision-maker pursues, and the QALY measures health — not anyone's whole welfare.
Does the QALY then still need risk neutrality and the rest?
Much less: it must be a good, agreed measure of health, not a perfect model of each person's choices.
Our example reads cleanly this way: 1.5 QALYs gained for 30,000 more — 20,000 per QALY, set against the payer's threshold λ.
The price is that the value judgements come into the open: the decision-maker, not the individual, chooses what counts.
So the QALY rests on one of two things: expected utility theory, if it is to be a utility, or a social choice to maximise health, if it is not.
Now you can see what an argument about QALYs is often really about — which of those two foundations the speaker stands on.
